news_drafts.headline: Flintshire: none of its £18.95m of LOBO bank loans was called in the six months to September 2026
news_drafts.lead:
None of Flintshire Council's £18.95m of LOBO loans was called in the six months to September 2026, according to papers for its Governance and Audit Committee meeting on 24 November. A LOBO is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The council held the £18.95m on 1 April 2026, and all of it had semi-annual call dates in that period.

The papers say the loans also have call dates within the next 12 months, and that the council has liaised with the firm Arlingclose on the likelihood of the options being exercised. If a lender proposed a revised rate, the council says it "plans to repay the loan at no additional cost as accepting the revised terms would mean the Council would still have refinancing risk in later years." Replacement funding would come from cash, other local authorities or the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils. The paper gives no figure for the cost of replacement funding.

A schedule of loans at 30 September 2026 lists the LOBO block at £18.95m, with annual interest of £858,095. The three loans carry rates of 4.48%, 4.53% and 4.58%, and mature between January 2040 and January 2042.

news_drafts.headline: Flintshire projects a £7.625m gross overspend at Month 6, down from £8.493m at Month 5
news_drafts.lead:
Flintshire Council is projecting a gross operating deficit of £7.625m on the Council Fund for 2026/27 at Month 6, according to a report to its Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee. Using the whole of the remaining £2.704m budget risk reserve would reduce that to a net deficit of £4.921m. The gross figure is £0.868m lower than the £8.493m reported at Month 5, with £1.800m released from deferred ultra-low emission vehicle infrastructure costs and a £0.507m grant set against fleet borrowing costs among the movements.

Out of County Placements are projected at £28.345m against a £25.706m budget, an overspend of £2.639m, even though £2m was added to the budget. The paper says further net placements are "highly likely". The rest of Social Services is projected at £122.275m against £117.240m, an overspend of £5.035m. Children's professional support teams are £0.625m overspent, largely from agency costs because of "challenges recruiting and retaining social workers". The council projects that 82% of its £10.999m of budget reductions will be achieved, leaving a £2.015m shortfall.

Unearmarked reserves are projected at £9.751m after the overspend, down from £18.261m at the start of the year. School reserves stood at a deficit of £4.798m at 31 March 2026, an adverse movement of £4.199m. The paper says school deficits are projected to exceed £8m by 31 March 2027. The 3.5% teachers' pay award from September 2026 compares with the 3.2% in the settlement and the 3.0% the council budgeted. Welsh Government grant covers part of the gap, and the paper says a residual shortfall "will need to be met from within existing resources".

news_drafts.headline: Flintshire's contingency reserve falls from £8.272m to £0.748m after one-off costs and a Month 5 forecast
news_drafts.lead:
Flintshire Council's contingency reserve, the money held back for the unexpected, is down to £0.748m from £8.272m, according to a paper before its Cabinet on 13 October 2026. The reserve is the part of its reserves, the money it has put aside, that sits above the base level the council keeps.

The largest call on it is a projected outturn of £5.789m at Month 5. Outturn is the actual spending figure for a year once it has ended, as against what was budgeted. Here it is a projection part-way through the year. The paper also sets out three one-off pressures the reserve is to fund: £0.142m for children's services legal costs, £0.165m to put in place SharePoint, a document-sharing software system, and £0.036m for temporary posts.

The four items named in the paper do not by themselves account for the whole fall from £8.272m to £0.748m. The material does not itemise the remainder. The paper's total line reads "Total Contingency Reserve 0.748".

findings.headline: One of the fund's property managers, Darwin, has had "significant decline in valuation" after specific performance and strategy issues.
findings.detail: The paper says Darwin has experienced some specific performance and strategy issues, which resulted in a significant decline in valuation. The paper does not give a figure for the decline.
findings.matters: A manager-level valuation decline within a property allocation is a risk that a finance officer at any fund holding the same manager would need to assess.
findings.quote: which resulted in a significant decline in valuation.

findings.headline: Total equity exposure is 39.6% of the fund, 4.6% above the 35.0% benchmark allocation, including synthetic equity of 22.0%.
findings.detail: The paper says synthetic global equity exposure is 22.0% as at 30 September 2026. It reports that total equity is 4.6% above the benchmark allocation.
findings.matters: A finance officer assessing equity-market exposure in a fund can compare the level of overweight against the benchmark and the synthetic share used to reach it.
findings.figures: Total equity exposure: 39.6%; benchmark: 35.0%; above benchmark: 4.6%; global synthetic equity: 22.0%

findings.headline: Cash is 7.7% of the fund under the Government SAA template, against an upper strategic bound of 7.0%, and WPP IM Co is to advise on it.
findings.detail: The paper says that on the adviser's own asset-class view cash is underweight at 2.8%, but under the Government SAA template it is overweight. It says WPP IM Co will provide advice on how to address the overweight.
findings.matters: Pension funds reporting to the Government SAA template can show a different position from their own strategic ranges, which a reader at another authority checking their own template figures would want to know.
findings.figures: Cash under SAA template: 7.7% vs upper strategic bound 7.0%; proposed upper range 5.0%; total strategic cash and liquidity: 2.8% of fund
findings.quote: Cash is overweight at 7.7%, versus the upper strategic bound of 7.0%.

findings.headline: Total Infrastructure is at 8.4% of the fund, against a 6.0% target and a 4.0–8.0% range, and the adviser is in discussion about widening the range.
findings.detail: The paper says infrastructure is overweight, mainly because of a top-up to the open-ended JP Morgan fund in July 2024. It says rebalancing is not straightforward because the other infrastructure assets are closed-ended. The adviser's discussions with WPP IM Co on widening the infrastructure control range, for example to ±3%, are ongoing.
findings.matters: A pension fund proposing to widen its own allocation control range in response to an illiquid overweight is a governance choice other funds with similar holdings may face.
findings.figures: Allocation: 8.4%; target: 6.0%; range: 4.0–8.0%; excess above upper range: 0.4%; overweight vs target: 2.4%
findings.quote: Total Infrastructure is marginally outside the range.

findings.headline: WPP Sustainable Active Equity returned 2.3% in the quarter to 30 September 2026 against a 1.9% benchmark.
findings.detail: The paper says the equity fund's one-year and three-year figures lag its benchmark, but its quarterly performance was ahead. It describes the fund as generally in line with or above the median manager in the sustainable active manager universe.
findings.matters: It shows a manager ahead of its benchmark in the latest quarter while its longer-run record still trails, which a finance officer reviewing manager mandates would want to see.
findings.figures: Quarter: 2.3% vs 1.9% benchmark; 1 year: 19.8% vs 20.1%; 3 years: 14.3% vs 19.2% (p.a.)
findings.quote: with quarterly performance being ahead of the benchmark in Q3 2026.

daily_post.headline: The council's loan book to wholly owned companies is within its self-assessed £38m cash limit, which the paper says covers loans to its housing subsidiary NEW Homes
daily_post.lead: A council that lends to its own housing company at a set margin over PWLB, with a self-assessed cap, shows a lending structure that finance directors and lenders may want to compare.
